# Racial and ethnic inequities in the quality of paediatric care in the USA: a review of quantitative evidence

**Authors:** Natalie Slopen; Andrew R Chang; Tiffani J Johnson; Ashaunta T Anderson; Aleha M Bate; Shawnese Clark; Alyssa Cohen; Monique Jindal; J’Mag Karbeah; Lee M Pachter; Naomi Priest; Shakira F Suglia; Nessa Bryce; Andrea Fawcett; Nia Heard-Garris

## Abstract

Racial and ethnic inequities in paediatric care have received increased research attention over the past two decades, particularly in the past 5 years, alongside an increased societal focus on racism. In this Series paper, the first in a two-part Series focused on racism and child health in the USA, we summarise evidence on racial and ethnic inequities in the quality of paediatric care. We review studies published between Jan 1, 2017 and July 31, 2022, that are adjusted for or stratified by insurance status to account for group differences in access, and we exclude studies in which differences in access are probably driven by patient preferences or the appropriateness of intervention. Overall, the literature reveals widespread patterns of inequitable treatment across paediatric specialties, including neonatology, primary care, emergency medicine, inpatient and critical care, surgery, developmental disabilities, mental health care, endocrinology, and palliative care. The identified studies indicate that children from minoritised racial and ethnic groups received poorer health-care services relative to non-Hispanic White children, with most studies drawing on data from multiple sites, and accounting for indicators of family socioeconomic position and clinical characteristics (eg, comorbidities or condition severity). The studies discussed a range of potential causes for the observed disparities, including implicit biases and differences in site of care or clinician characteristics. We outline priorities for future research to better understand and address paediatric treatment inequities and implications for practice and policy. Policy changes within and beyond the health-care system, discussed further in the second paper of this Series, are essential to address the root causes of treatment inequities and to promote equitable and excellent health for all children.

## Introduction

Racial and ethnic disparities in health are substantial and persistent in the USA,1,2 present in the earliest years of life and shaped by structural racism. Racism, a multidimensional system of oppression that unfairly structures opportunities and resources to disadvantage children from minoritised racial and ethnic groups,3,4 profoundly impacts children’s health5–9 throughout their lives.10 In 2010, the American Academy of Pediatrics Committee on paediatric research published a landmark comprehensive report on racial and ethnic disparities in children’s health and health care in the USA,11 concluding that inequalities are pervasive across outcomes and across the health-care continuum. Given the emphasis on improving equity in health care and beyond over the past two decades1,11–13 and the surge of scholarly activity in this area, this Series offers an updated and focused review on health-care inequities (paper 1) and policy solutions14 (paper 2) to eliminate racial and ethnic disparities in the USA. We have adopted the definition of a health-care treatment disparity as specified in the Institute of Medicine’s 2002 Unequal Treatment report: “differences in the quality of health care that are not due to access-related factors or clinical needs, preferences, and appropriateness of intervention”.15 Our review relies on categorising children into racial and ethnic groups, which is inherently over-simplistic and requires use of a social classification system with no biological validity; however, documenting differences in paediatric health-care quality across groups is crucial to bring change to this inequity.

This Series is guided by an ecological model of racism (figure) that emphasises the role that societal structures and systems—including health care, education, housing, and legal and economic systems—play in shaping the social, physical, and interpersonal environment and interactions children experience, inclusive of both implicit and overt racism. Together, these structures, systems, and downstream environments and interactions influence a child’s opportunity for healthy development. The overarching aim of the Series is to highlight structural sources of inequitable environments for children, with this Series paper focusing on paediatric health-care specialties. The disparities in health care are the result of compounding systems within the broader ecosystem that create, sustain, and perpetuate inequities in quality of care, access, and preferences (figure).

We review studies from the USA that have been published in the past 5 years to maintain a reasonable scope and because of the importance of focusing on the most recent evidence available, although some studies used data from much earlier. We focus on differences in care that cannot be clearly accounted for by access (proxied via insurance status),15 preference, or medical need; these differences will be referred to as treatment inequities throughout the Series paper. Given our definition of a health-care treatment disparity, we limit our review to studies that either adjust for or stratify by insurance status or restrict enrolment to a single-payer health care (eg, Medicaid), thereby offering a unique contribution to the paediatric health inequities literature. We recognise this is an imperfect control for differences in access to care, as health insurance plans can vary with regard to services covered and availability of practitioners and appointments. Notably, access to insurance (both public and private) is shaped by structural racism and other systemic inequities; however, a focus on disparities in insurance and related sequelae are beyond the scope of this Series paper. Specifically, we excluded outcomes focused on access issues, cost, or health outcomes not directly tied to the quality of care. We also strived to exclude outcomes directly influenced by patient or parent preferences, recognising that there is ambiguity in the role of preference even among some of the included studies. The empirical studies that we review are summarised in the appendix (pp 2–29). Throughout, we use the terminology for racial and ethnic groups as used within the study being described.

First, we review studies on health-care treatment inequities within each paediatric specialty. In accordance with other quality of care research,16,17 we focus on structural measures (ie, the context in which care takes place, such as provider capacity and systems to provide high quality care), process measures (ie, transactions between providers and patients during care, including technical or interpersonal activities to maintain or improve patient health), and outcome measures (ie, the impact of care on the patient’s or population’s health status), to the extent evidence is available. We review neonatology, the earliest form of paediatric specialty care, specialties based on the setting of care (eg, primary care, emergency medicine, inpatient and critical care, and surgical care), and specialties focused on the treatment of specific health conditions (eg, developmental disabilities and other special health-care needs, mental health care, endocrinology, and palliative care). Second, we consider the general patterns across specialties, the rigor and breadth of the existing research, and mechanisms for the observed patterns. Finally, we consider the implications of these results for future research, practice, and policy.

## Neonatology

There are well documented and enduring racial and ethnic disparities in the quality of prenatal care,18,19 with implications for neonatal outcomes. Inequitable outcomes in neonatal hospital care have received substantial research attention in recent years.20–25 We focus on neonatal health-care quality measures that were selected by a panel of experts.26 Overall, the literature aligns with a systematic review inclusive of studies until March, 2018,27 which found complex patterns of racial and ethnic disparities in structures (eg, nursing characteristics and racially segregated hospitals), processes (eg, facilitation of breastfeeding in the hospital, follow-ups, and referrals), and outcomes (eg, hospital morbidity and mortality) that typically disadvantage infants from minoritised racial and ethnic groups, particularly Black infants.

Considering the most recent literature, numerous studies show excess risk for worse quality of care for infants from minoritised racial and ethnic groups relative to White infants.20,22–24 One study of very low birthweight infants found that relative to non-Hispanic White infants, non-Hispanic Black infants and Native American infants are less likely to have received any human milk at hospital discharge.23 Asian and Pacific Islander infants were more likely to have received any human milk at hospital discharge, and the degree of disparities varied considerably across regions and states.23 Disparities in human milk provision cannot be attributed to preference alone, as research shows racial disparities in access to maternity care practices that support breastfeeding.28

Studies of outcome measures show similar patterns. A study of 438 834 low-risk newborns from 40 hospitals in New York City (NY) found that unexpected newborn complications (defined as potentially avoidable serious or moderate complications) were higher among Hispanic and non-Hispanic Black infants relative to non-Hispanic White infants.20 Another study of 19 325 preterm infants from 12 clinical sites found that sepsis, but not neonatal death, was higher among non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic neonates relative to non-Hispanic White neonates.24 Although few studies have examined time trends in neonatal health-care quality disparities, there is some evidence from a study of 25 academic medical centres that racial and ethnic disparities in late-onset sepsis and receipt of antenatal corticosteroids among extremely preterm infants (<28 weeks gestation) improved between 2002 and 2016.25

## Specialties based on setting of care

### Primary care

Primary care is a key point of access for many children and families seeking health-care services. Racial and ethnic disparities in the delivery of paediatric medical home services have been well documented29,30 and persist in the literature focused on processes and outcomes in general primary care31–34 and asthma care,35,36 although patterns are inconsistent. Considering process of care outcomes, several studies have focused on communication within primary care. A study focused on provider recommendation of human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination within a longitudinal cohort found that among parents reporting low levels of patient-centred care (but not among those reporting high levels of patient-centred care), parents of non-Hispanic Black children had significantly lower odds of receiving a recommendation for HPV vaccination for their child than parents of non-Hispanic White children.32 Similarly, a study of adolescents in the National Survey of Children’s Health found that caregivers of White adolescents were more likely to report that their adolescent received risk counselling relative to reports from caregivers of children from other racial or ethnic groups.34 In an analysis of 5390 children age 6–12 years, the Medical Expenditures Panel Survey did not identify racial and ethnic differences across four measures of parent–provider communication quality.37

Studies focused on asthma care processes also indicate mixed results.35,36 One study used electronic health record data from 37 614 children with asthma with a primary care visit in 21 states, revealing Latino children had lower odds than non-Hispanic White children of having their asthma recorded on their problem list on the first day the diagnosis was noted, which might delay appropriate care at future visits. However, there was no difference in the rate of asthma severity documentation on the patient’s problem list.35 Similarly, based on parent-reported survey data from 647 families in the Population-Based Effectiveness in Asthma and Lung Diseases Network, Black children were less likely to have a written asthma treatment plan given or reviewed by a provider than their White peers; however, there were no differences observed in the frequency of asthma medication review.36

Considering outcome measures, some of the literature shows over-screening in minoritised children. One study found that temperature measurement at well-child visits was more common among Hispanic and Black children relative to non-Hispanic White children,33 which could lead to overdiagnosis, recognised as potentially harmful to children.38 A study using data from a network of 31 paediatric primary care clinics found that non-Hispanic Black adolescents had significantly higher odds of chlamydia screening than their non-Hispanic White peers; this difference remained even after adjusting for individual, clinician, and clinic-based characteristics.31

### Emergency medicine

The emergency department is the clinical area with the most publications showing paediatric disparities over the past 5 years. Disparities in emergency medicine are particularly concerning given the important role of the emergency department as a health-care safety net, where marginalised populations can access care regardless of insurance status or ability to pay.39 The literature shows disparities in structural measures, such as waiting times at the emergency department.40,41 Disparities that disadvantage minoritised children are also evident in process measures such as assignment of triage acuity.41–43 Evaluation for suspected child abuse is another process measure in emergency care for which disparities have been widely reported. In a 2018 systematic review44 of skeletal surveys in young, injured children (at age <60 months), five of six studies45–50 examining racial disparities found that Black and Hispanic children were more likely to be evaluated with a skeletal survey than White children.

Considering disparities in outcome measures within paediatric emergency medicine, the most robust evidence exists in pain management.51–57 Disparities have been documented in the provision of opioid analgesics for children presenting with any painful condition56 and specifically among those with objective diagnoses, such as long bone fractures,51–53,55,57 appendicitis,51–57 and migraines.58 Findings of disparities in pain management for children with fractures are consistent with previous research investigating disparities in paediatric trauma care, such as the management of supracondylar fractures59 and replanting an amputated digit,60 as highlighted in a 2019 systematic review.61

Beyond treatment of more stigmatised conditions, such as child abuse, the literature on opioids,51–57 antibiotics,62,63 intravenous fluids,64 and diagnostic imaging41,65–68 suggest an overall trend of more care for White patients. This trend is seen even for care that is not evidence based, such as antibiotics for viral illness,62,63 chest x-rays and laboratory testing for asthma and bronchiolitis,65,67 and other low-value care (ie, services where the potential for harm exceeds benefits, such as imaging for constipation or headache69). A single-centre study found that Black and Hispanic children and children of other races were less likely to receive intravenous fluids for gastroenteritis and dehydration than White children, despite guidance from a clinical care pathway.64

By contrast, there was also evidence that standardised protocols within the emergency department can reduce disparate treatment relative to clinical judgement alone.70 The general pattern of less treatment for minoritised children was also found for procedures41 and subspecialty consultations71 in the emergency department, and minoritised children are more likely to leave the emergency department without complete evaluation or care.72 Potential undertreatment in Black children can affect outcomes; for example, a delayed diagnosis of appendicitis increases the risk of ruptured appendicitis.68 Finally, there was some evidence to suggest intersections of race with age and sex.43,56,71 In one sample in which fever was the chief complaint at the emergency department, racial disparities in triage score was only evident in children older than 1 year.43

### Critical and inpatient hospital care

The literature on racial and ethnic disparities in paediatric critical and inpatient care quality73–79 shows evidence of inequitable care across some studies, with mixed results. Considering studies of process measures, a study of 424 adolescents who had posterior spinal fusion for idiopathic scoliosis at a single institution documented disparities in postoperative pain before implementing a coordinated care pathway; following implementation, these differences were eliminated.79 Another study of 91 549 children found non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic children were less likely than non-Hispanic White patients with similar asthma acuity to receive chest x-rays in inpatient and emergency encounters.73 Two studies of asthma-related hospitalisations indicated no racial differences in 30-day all-cause revisit rates74 or referral to an asthma specialist,75 although non-Hispanic Black children were less likely than non-Hispanic White children to receive a written asthma action plan.75 Another study included 904 families with children who were inpatients at a paediatric tertiary care hospital and found that, relative to parents of White patients, parents of non-White patients reported lower satisfaction related to family-centred care, patient–provider relationships, and cultural competency across all provider types; meanwhile, there were no disparities in satisfaction related to hospital systems, processes, and infrastructure.76

Studies of outcome measures within critical and inpatient hospital care also found patterns that disadvantage minoritised children. A study of 3231 patients from 16 hospitals examined racial and ethnic disparities in inpatient adverse events from medical records and found that Latino patients were more likely to have preventable and high-severity adverse events relative to White patients.77

### Surgery

Some,80,81 but not all,82 studies of racial and ethnic disparities in the quality of surgical care for children indicate differences in care, mostly within the domain of outcome measures. In a study of 100 639 children in the Nationwide Inpatient Sample who had an appendicectomy, perioperative complications were consistently higher for Black children compared with White children, with no evidence of the racial disparity gap narrowing over time, controlling for clinical characteristics including perforated appendicitis status, laparoscopy status, and number of comorbidities.80 Similarly, in a study of 66 157 children in the Healthcare Cost and Use Project Kids’ Inpatient Database who had inpatient gastrointestinal surgical procedures, Black and Native American children and children classified as other races had elevated odds of postoperative complications relative to White children.80 By contrast, a study of 786 children undergoing laparoscopic appendicectomy at a single hospital found that the mean postoperative length of stay was similar among Black, Hispanic, and White children.82

## Subspecialties focused on childhood conditions

### Developmental disability and children with special health-care needs

Racial and ethnic disparities in process measures for childhood developmental disabilities have been noted,83–85 and the recent literature is consistent with previous reports.86–92 Data from 7950 children from the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study-Birth Cohort show that Black and Asian children were less likely than White children to be diagnosed with a developmental disability by preschool (aged 4 years) or kindergarten (aged 5–6 years), even after controlling for scores on formal developmental assessments.92 Similarly, a study using a national sample of children with special health-care needs found that Latino children received fewer specialty services than non-Hispanic White children, with this disparity moderated by physician responsiveness to parental concerns (ie, a passive or reassuring response was associated with Latino children receiving fewer services than non-Hispanic White children).87

Likewise, a study using administrative data to examine children with autism spectrum disorder who have Medicaid insurance documented racial and ethnic differences across all minoritised groups for nine common autism-related services, with patterns of disparities varying across types of services.86 Black, Asian, and Native American or Pacific Islander children received fewer outpatient services than White children, but there was no disparity for Latinx children; at the same time, Black and Asian children received more school-based services than White children. The contrasting patterns for outpatient and school-based services could be driven by geography (ie, in metro areas with large minoritised child populations, children might have easier access to school-based services compared with outpatient services) or discriminatory practices that result in a higher likelihood for minority children to be placed in special education and, therefore, to receive services that can be billed to Medicaid.86

Finally, several studies focused on care quality among parents of children with special health-care needs, all using data from the 2009–10 National Survey of Children with Special Health Care Needs.88–91 Each study found evidence that compared with parents of White children, parents from minoritised racial and ethnic groups reported lower quality of care in terms of family-centred care,89,91 parent satisfaction with care,90 and care coordination.88

### Mental health specialty care

Studies that examined racial or ethnic disparities in the quality of paediatric mental health-care services93–100 consistently provide at least some evidence of disparate treatment disadvantaging children from minoritised racial and ethnic groups, with most studies focused on process measures. In a study of Medicaid data from four states examining disparities in processes of care, the reduction of antidepressant prescribing following the Food and Drug Administration box warning about increased suicide ideation was slower among providers treating large numbers of minoritised children than those treating small numbers of minoritised children.93 Black and Latino patients and their White peers were treated by largely separate providers whose responses to the box warning differed, with providers treating predominantly White patients responding faster than those treating predominantely minority patients.93

One study included 819 patients at five hospitals and found that African American children with suicidality were less likely to have documentation of caregiver counselling on lethal means restriction before discharge (ie, how to restrict access to lethal means of suicide, such as firearms, medications, and cars) relative to their White counterparts.94 However, disparities were not present across the other eight indicators of mental health-care quality, such as mental health assessment and substance use screening in emergency departments, timely consultations, and discharge communication with an outpatient provider for inpatients (appendix p 30). Three studies using Medicaid data focused on children with major depressive disorder diagnoses,96,98,99 finding lower rates of minimally adequate care for minoritised children relative to non-Hispanic White children.

Other studies of Medicaid data have identified disparities in quality of care related to outpatient mental health service use following a traumatic brain injury97 and complex differences in adequate treatment for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).95 Finally, in a national survey of 2401 children with ADHD, non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic, and children classified as other were less likely than non-Hispanic White children to have ever received ADHD medication, and Hispanic children were less likely than non-Hispanic White children to be receiving medications for ADHD.100

### Endocrinology

Research on racial and ethnic disparities in endocrinology care has focused on use of growth hormones101,102 and diabetes care.103,104 We recognise that within this specialty area in particular, deciphering between quality and preference is challenging; we erred on the side of being overly inclusive since preferences are shaped by experiences within the health-care system.15 Studies of paediatric growth hormone use to treat short stature have documented that non-Hispanic White children are more likely than non-Hispanic Black or Hispanic children to receive growth hormone treatment.101,102 For diabetes care, relative to non-Hispanic White children, non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic children were less likely to be treated with an insulin pump,103,104 and non-Hispanic Black children were less likely to have continuous glucose monitoring,103 even after controlling for insurance status.

### Palliative care

A few studies focused on racial and ethnic disparities in health-care quality among children experiencing end-of-life care.105–107 Considering process measures, a study of 1193 children from the Pediatric Health Information System database who had undergone stem-cell transplantation found that Hispanic children were 59% less likely then non-Hispanic White children to receive inpatient palliative care consultations; no differences were evident for other racial groups.107 Considering outcome measures, two studies used administrative data on deaths in California to identify children with cancer (n=3732)105 and complex chronic conditions (n=8654)106 and found that relative to non-Hispanic White children, Black, Hispanic, and Asian American children were more likely to have a hospital death,105 and Hispanic children were more likely to have medically intense care within the last days of life.105,106 These disparities have consequences for patients and their families, given that high-intensity care is associated with worse caregiver outcomes.108,109

### Other subspecialty care

Little research within the study period focuses on racial and ethnic disparities in paediatric care within specialties of neurology,110 oncology,111 otolaryngology,112 and urological medicine.113 Considering paediatric neurology, in a study of 247 children with epilepsy, Hispanic children had a lower likelihood of seizure remission relative to non-Hispanic White children, despite no differences between these two groups of children in the number of antiseizure medication prescriptions, types of anti-seizure medications, or proportion of days covered by these prescriptions, thus the disparity is not explained by prescribing or refill patterns.110 Another study found that non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic Black, and White Hispanic children were less likely to be diagnosed with a leukodystrophy relative to non-Hispanic White children, even though leukodystrophy disease-associated allele frequencies were the same or higher in populations of Latino or African descent.114 One otolaryngology study that included 1511 children in Florida who had cochlear implantation found that non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic children were less likely than White children to receive a cochlear implant younger than 2 years,112 adding to a growing body of evidence on disparities in paediatric otolaryngology care.115,116

## Discussion

Across paediatric specialties, the literature in the past 5 years on racial and ethnic disparities in paediatric health-care quality describes pervasive inequities in the health-care quality received by children in the USA. Notably, the studies included in this review all controlled for or stratified by insurance status to minimise differences attributable to access. Overall, the research designs were strong: half of the studies included control variables for socioeconomic position beyond insurance status, a large majority included control variables for clinical characteristics (eg, comorbidities or condition severity), and many studies used data collected from multiple sites, thus increasing generalisability. Although a few studies reported complex patterns, most studies reported patterns of inequitable care that disadvantage children from minoritised racial and ethnic groups relative to non-Hispanic White children or overserve non-Hispanic White children for at least one study outcome.

Several studies included time trend analyses,25,57,80 documenting promising patterns of attenuating disparities in quality of care for some outcomes (eg, opioid prescription disparities for long bone fractures57 and neonatal late-onset sepsis)25 but not others (surgical complications for children with appendicitis).80 Of the identified studies, only a few21,37,82,110 reported null findings across all study outcomes; however, null studies are less likely to be published than other studies due to publication bias. Samples were collected from patients from diverse geographical areas and medical settings and from administrative records; we could not discern any patterns based on geography that could account for discrepancies across studies, and further work should consider disparities related to regional and other geographical factors. Finally, our review indicates that experiences of Asian American and Native American children, and those classified as multiethnic or multiracial, were less represented within the existing literature relative to other groups of children.

Eliminating the contribution of access-related constraints and family preference to the observed disparities was impossible, and this proved a challenge to our review. Although all included studies adjusted for insurance status, different types of insurance might confer different levels of access to care, so it is an imperfect control. Furthermore, families belonging to minoritised racial and ethnic groups might experience more substantial structural constraints that obstruct engagement in optimal care (eg, less access to paid family and medical leave117 and transportation). Although we excluded outcomes that are highly likely to be driven by patient or family preference (eg, outcomes related to high-quality psychiatric care), we erred on the side of inclusion, given that preference is influenced by the quality and content of communication with providers, as well as historical events or discriminatory personal experiences that undermine trust or ability to engage with the medical system, even when accounting for insurance status.15 We did not identify studies of health-care disparities that met our inclusion criteria during the review period for several specialty areas (eg, anesthesiology, dermatology, neurosurgical care, and ophthalmology). Across several of these specialties, we identified articles documenting disparities in outcomes, treatment utilisation, and accessing care, but no studies met our inclusion criteria.111,118–120

The studies included in this review discussed a range of potential root causes for the observed disparities, such as biases and stereotyping as possible causes for providers’ clinical decisions.31,40,57,64,67,70,86,92,93,98 The interactions between patients and providers—including clinical decisions—are shaped by upstream systems and structures (figure), thus reflecting multiple intervention points to improve equity in care. Several studies used a before–after design and showed that guidelines and protocols within health-care settings support equal treatment.70,79 Some studies examined whether the site of care could explain the disparities in treatment quality (eg, size and racial composition of the practice).20,31,40,93 Other studies tested whether differences in treatment were related to the characteristics of the providers, such as responsiveness to concerns,87 provision of patient-centred care,32 specialty training,31,98 or years of experience.31 Distal structural factors, including housing, education, employment, and criminal justice, and the racism that underpins these factors are recognised as fundamental drivers of health-care disparities.121 However, these factors were infrequently given extensive discussion within the studies identified. Only a portion of studies named racism as the suggested mechanism for the inequities in quality of care. Potential policy solutions to address these upstream factors are discussed in the second paper in this Series.14

Qualitative approaches to understand parental perspectives of experiences of racism in health-care might help to generate solutions that paediatricians and others can implement in partnership with families and communities.122 Although our review was limited to quantitative studies, qualitative research can be superior for understanding patient perceptions and experiences of care. Two qualitative studies have identified ineffective communication and neglectful and judgmental care for Black and Hispanic families with infants receiving neonatal intensive care.123,124

## Implications for research, practice, and policy

Inequitable treatment is pervasive across paediatric care contexts. An ecological model of racism can inform strategies for eliminating this elevated risk of receiving inferior care among children from minoritised racial and ethnic groups. Building on these findings, we propose six specific research recommendations (panel).

First, we need additional and ongoing research to clarify the discrepant results observed for specific outcomes covered in this review and evaluate changes over time.

Second, concerted efforts to understand and intervene on the drivers of provider decision making that perpetuate inequitable treatment need to be developed, tested, disseminated, and scaled. Although research has shown that paediatric providers have implicit racial bias,125 little research has directly linked implicit bias with disparities in treatment decisions, patient satisfaction, or outcomes.126,127 Furthermore, evidence suggests that existing interventions related to implicit biases generally do not lead to sustained change in clinical behaviours or learning environments, thus emphasising the importance of structural changes within and beyond the health-care system.128

Third, more work is needed to characterise the experiences of Asian American and Native American children and of children belonging to multiple racial and ethnic groups. Given the heterogeneity within the broad racial and ethnic categories that are typically considered, disaggregation of subgroups whenever possible is crucial to provide accurate information for specific groups, thus ensuring that interventions and policies address the unique challenges faced by each group.129

Fourth, the next wave of research should investigate the intersection of race and ethnicity with other sociodemographic characteristics such as sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, family immigration history, language proficiency, and measures of socioeconomic position.130 Intersecting forms of inequity are important to document and address; for example, parent–provider language concordance might contribute to paediatric quality of care outcomes.131,132

Fifth, although there is some evidence that treatment algorithms can reduce paediatric health-care disparities,70 the full potential of technological innovations and other quality improvement strategies for reducing racial and ethnic disparities across paediatric specialties is unclear.122 There are complex technical and ethical considerations related to the introduction of treatment algorithms and machine learning-based models,133,134 many of which rely on incomplete information related to social and structural contexts, learning from and calibrating against bias, and overly relying on biological data available via electronic records;135 therefore, caution is needed.

Finally, there is an urgent need for research to identify strategies to intervene on systemic causes of health-care inequities (eg, access to care, institutional type, location, and quality of care) that are shaped by historical and present-day injustices within core societal systems, including housing, education, and employment.121,136 Some multisite studies reported that racial and ethnic differences in treatment could be explained by the site of care40 or largely different providers treating White and non-White children.93 Accordingly, we require evidence-informed approaches to redesign existing policies that systematically deny minoritised children and their families access to the same opportunities and services as their White counterparts.

Our review also has implications for practice and policy (panel). First, hospitals and other health-care systems should investigate sources of structural racism within their policies and guidelines. Policies should be reviewed with an equity-focused anti-racism lens to identify and address obstacles to high-quality care that systematically sustain disparate treatment.137,138 Second, senior management of health-care systems and providers must take steps to eliminate race-based paediatric care,139 as outlined in a position statement by the American Academy of Pediatrics.140 Third, health-care practices should adopt equity metrics as a part of quality improvement and safety portfolios136 and conduct recurrent audits with feedback to providers. Fourth, policy changes to end racial segregation of paediatric care141–143 and to enhance the diversity of the medical workforce144 are needed, which could have a meaningful influence on disparities in quality of care.145,146 Fifth, integration of community health workers as team members within the health-care workforce might bolster health-related outcomes among minoritised populations.147 Finally, policy changes extrinsic to the health-care system are essential to address the root causes that create and perpetuate disparities.14

## Conclusions

There are widespread inequities in treatment across many paediatric care specialties. Our review of recent literature reveals an urgent need to develop and implement effective interventions, including coordinated health care and cross-sectoral strategies that fundamentally redesign systems and policies to promote equitable and excellent health for all children. Extending on this conclusion, the second paper14 of this Series provides an overview of the status of inequities within intersecting systems that shape child health, including housing, employment, health insurance, the criminal legal system, and immigration and outlines promising policy solutions to address racism embedded within these systems.

# Mental health help-seeking willingness among U.S. college students: A resilience factor associated with many sexual minority identities

**Authors:** Andrew R. Chang; Ritika Rastogi; Genevieve Alice Woolverton; Justin A. Chen; Courtney Stevens; Sari L. Reisner; Cindy H. Liu

**Affiliations:** aHarvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts | bDepartments of Pediatric Newborn Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts | cNew York-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell Medical Center, New York City, New York | dDepartment of Psychology, Willamette University, Salem, Oregon | eThe Fenway Institute, Fenway Health, Boston, Massachusetts | fHarvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts | gDepartments of Pediatric Newborn Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts

## Abstract

For populations with elevated mental health risks such as college students and minority group, understanding openness to seeking professional help can be helpful to improve service engagement. This study explores help-seeking willingness among U.S. college students by sexual orientation.

Data were drawn from the 2021 National College Health Assessment (N=64,079). The main outcome of interest was help-seeking willingness, or reported openness to seeking professional mental health help when needed. A secondary outcome was help-seeking history, or past mental health service utilization. Logistic regression analyses were conducted using R version 4.0.5.

Increased help-seeking willingness was detected among students with a help-seeking history, whether within the past 12 months (OR=7.4, 99%CI: 6.78–9.08) or beyond (OR=2.26, 99%CI: 2.11–2.42). Even after controlling for help-seeking history, elevated odds of help-seeking willigness persisted for gay (AOR=2.01, 99%CI: 1.63–2.49), bisexual (AOR=1.35, 99%CI: 1.23–1.49), questioning (AOR=1.22, 99%CI: 1.04–1.45), pansexual (AOR=1.31, 99%CI: 1.06–1.63), and queer (AOR=1.78, 99%CI: 1.35–2.38), relative to heterosexual students.

Help-seeking willingness is a mental health resilience factor unique to several sexual minority groups. Examining what yields greater help-seeking willingness for these sexual minority student groups may inform interventions that enable all college students to seek help when they are in distress.

## INTRODUCTION

In a recent study, over half of college students met diagnostic criteria for a mental health problem, and a quarter of students screened positive for suicidality 1,2. Despite needs, individuals may not always seek help when they are in distress 3–5. In fact, more severe symptoms of mental distress may decrease help-seeking behavior 6,7. Unmet mental health needs confer deadly consequences (i.e., suicide), and prevention interventions must be aimed at connecting students to help when they are in distress and increasing help-seeking behavior 8,9.

Help-seeking can be understood from three dimensions: willingness, intention, and behavioral history. Much of the research literature focuses on the intended use of help given a current health issue (help-seeking intention) or an action or service utilization that has already occurred (help-seeking history) 2,10. However, studying help-seeking intention or history alone fail to capture the behavioral risks of most college students. College students are prone to help-needing distress during this developmental period, but many students do not carry a mental health diagnosis or utilization history11. As many students have no previous experience with professional mental health care when they enter college, both help-seeking intention and history cannot predict how they will fare 12,13. A different approach is needed to understand the mental health help-seeking of the college population, as they learn when and how to seek help 2,5,14.

The concept of help-seeking willingness provides a comprehensive outlook on help-seeking by asking all individuals whether they would seek professional mental health help in a future scenario when they are in distress 15. Distinct from an intended or enacted use of help, help-seeking willingness portrays a general attitude and an anticipated openness toward asking for help. As help-seeking willingness positively correlate with intention, it can be conceptualized as an attiudinal precursor to intention11. One’s willingness may meaningfully promote their intention, which then yields beneficial help-seeking behaviors. In this way, help-seeking willingness is more encompassing, detecting help-seeking likelihood among all college students. Despite the innovative questions it answers, help-seeking willingness remains severely underexplored.

This study addresses the literature gap on college mental health and help-seeking behavior by focusing on help-seeking willingness. The limited number of studies have connected help-seeking willingness with mental health knowledge and cultural attitudes, social support structure, and metacognitive awareness of their mental health status 15. Institutional factors such as campus region and culture also influence help-seeking willigness. Specifically, a stigma-free campus norms may dispel attitudinal barriers and more accessible health services may increase preventative health awareness 16. Still, quantitative explorations on the strength of these relationships are lacking and warranted.

Furthermore, this study answers the call by prevention researchers call to focus on resilience factors as the foci for mental health intervention. After all, help-seeking willingness is a resilience factor as it promotes students to find help and overcome mental health challenges 17–20. Different student groups have different attitude to professional mental health services and their perceived effectiveness of provided help 2,6,21. Understanding help-seeking willingness can illuminate these attudinal differences and improve service accessibility by specific population groups 15,22. Services must engage student groups with high mental health needs but have low help-seeking willingness, either due to limited mental health awareness or poor perception of services. Researchers are particularly advocating for studies on resilience factors for minority groups, as most mental health research focus on their risk factors 18. This risk-based approach elides the unique strengths of minority communities.

Among minority student groups, sexual minority college students have particularly alarming rates of mental health needs 8,22. Their needs deserve focused attention, but most research studies aggregated lesbian, gay, bisexual, and queer (LGBQ+) groups or did not capture the sexual diversity in today’s youth 24. We use a diverse range of self-reported sexual identities and describe their help-seeking willingness. In previous studies focused on help-seeking history alone, sexual minority students report higher help-seeking history but also have disproportionately high mental health needs 25. Service needs confound most behavior and utilization history research, and among just college students with severe mental health challenge, fewer proportions of sexual minority students may in fact receive support relative to heterosexual students 11. It is reported that many sexual minority persons receive inferior care due to provider discrimination and stigma, which may further contribute as barriers to care 26–29. Understanding help-seeking willingness in addition to history illuminates whether sexual minority students are indeed more likely to seek help regardless of their service needs or past experiences.

Using the Spring 2021 National College Health Assessment (NCHA) data, this study examines help-seeking willingness and its predictors among college students. We include help-seeking history as a predictor to understand the relationship between help-seeking history and willingness. With a large sample size, we assess meaningful differences in help-seeking willingness by sexual orientation and how these differences change after considering help-seeking history.

## METHODS

### Data Source

The NCHA is a cross-sectional survey administered twice per year by the American College Health Association. Respondents voluntarily self-report various individual, campus, and mental health characteristics. The Spring 2021 NCHA was administered entirely online to undergraduate and graduate students aged 18 years or above across 137 U.S. postsecondary institutions. The average response rate was 13%, consistent with previous years of survey administration. We employed complete case analysis and removed respondents who reported implausible height and weight data based on a protocol described elsewhere 30. The final sample used in the analysis included 64,079 degree-seeking undergraduate students, reflecting 9% data loss from the original sample.

### Sexual Orientation

Sexual orientation was self-reported by student respondents. Ten options were included in the survey: “asexual”, “bisexual”, “gay”, “lesbian”, “pansexual”, “queer”, “questioning”, “same gender loving”, “straight/heterosexual”, or “another identity”. There were no respondents who self-identified as “same gender loving” so the final sexual orientation included nine groups. As the heterosexual category was overrepresented in the sample, this category was used as the reference group for regression analyses on sexual orientations.

### Help-Seeking Willingness

The primary outcome was measured with the question “if in the future you were having a personal problem that was really bothering you, would you consider seeking help from a mental health professional?” (yes/no).

### Help-Seeking History

The secondary outcome of this study was determined based on two questions, “have you ever received psychological or mental health services?” (yes/no) and “within the last 12 months, have you received psychological or mental health services?” (yes/no). Based on the responses, participants were characterized as those with beyond-12-month history (yes to ever receiving service but no to receiving services within the last 12 months), within-12-month history (yes to both questions), or never sought help (no to ever receiving service). In regression analysis, this three-category variable was converted to two separate binary outcomes: 12-month (only respondents endorsing within-12-month history) and lifetime (respondents endorsing either within-12-month or beyond-12-month history) help-seeking history.

### Covariates

#### Individual Characteristics

The self-reported age was dichotomized into 18 to 24 years old and 25 years old or above based on a previously validated approach 31,32. Recoded gender identity included eight groups: man, woman, transgender, genderqueer, agender, genderfluid, nonbinary, and other. To strike a balance between representation and analytic power, Green’s procedure was used. Both transgender woman and transgender man groups had fewer than 130 respondents (N > 50 + 8 covariates * (10)) and were collapsed 33. Race and ethnicity response included 7 groups: White, Asian, Hispanic, Black, Native American or Pacific Islander (NAPI), Multiracial, and Other. The insurance status was categorized as school-based, private which included coverage based on parent/guardian’s plan, public, other which included not being sure about the source of the insurance, and no insurance.

#### Campus Characteristics

College regions included the Northeast, the Midwest, the South, and the West. College types included public and private. Campus mental health culture was generated based on students’ responses to their level of agreement with four statements, “I feel that I belong at my college/university”, “I feel that students’ health and well-being is a priority at my college/university”, “at my college/university, I feel that the campus climate encourages free and open discussions about students’ health and well-being”, and “at my college/university, we are a campus where we look out for each other”. The level of agreement was rated on a 6-item Likert scale (where 6 was “strongly agree” and 1 was “strongly disagree”). The cumulative campus culture score was converted into a binary outcome: negative with scores 4–16 and positive with scores 17–24.

#### Mental Health Characteristics

Mental health distress level was described by the Kessler 6 scale, which rated the number of days the respondent experienced various mental health symptoms within a week 34. The scale was converted to a three-category measure of mild (0–5), moderate (6–12), and severe (13–24) psychological distress based on validated score cut-offs 35. The Suicide Behavior Questionnaire-Revised Screening scored respondents from 3 to 18, based on their prior attempts and current suicidal ideation, thoughts, and behaviors. A score of 7 or above indicated a positive screen for high suicide risk based on a previous validation study 36.

### Data Analysis

Analyses were performed in three steps. First, we presented the individual, campus, and mental health characteristics in the overall sample and by sexual orientation. Second, we performed bivariate analysis to describe the associations between our primary outcome of help-seeking willingness and characteristics including help-seeking history. Third, we described the odds of help-seeking willingness by sexual orientation. Two adjustment models were employed: Model 1 adjusted for individual, campus, and mental health characteristics, while Model 2 adjusted for all characteristics in Model 1 as well as help-seeking history. Finally, multilevel logistic regression analyses described the associations between help-seeking history and sexual orientation. Data analyses were performed using R version 4.0.5 (2021). Associations estimated at p < 0.01 were considered statistically significant.

## RESULTS

The distribution of individual, campus, and mental health characteristics among all sexual orientation groups is displayed in Table 1. Severe psychological distress and positive suicide risk were disproportionately over-represented in all sexual minority groups.

### Individual Predictors of Help-Seeking Willingness

In Table 2, bivariate logistic regression analyses assessed the associations between help-seeking willingness and various individual, campus, and mental health characteristics. Among studied covariates, the strongest predictor for help-seeking willingness was having a positive help-seeking history, whether within 12 months (odds ratio [OR]=7.40, 99% confidence interval [CI]: 6.78–8.09) or beyond (OR=2.26, 99%CI: 2.11–2.42) relative to never receiving mental health services. Relative to heterosexual students, all sexual minority students except non-heterosexual other, had elevated odds of help-seeking willingness (gay: OR=1.64, 99%CI: 1.35–2.00; lesbian: OR=1.76, 99%CI: 1.44–2.16; bisexual: OR=1.76, 99%CI: 1.76–2.10; questioning: OR=1.51, 99%CI: 1.30–1.77; pansexual: OR=2.02, 99%CI: 1.66–2.48; queer: OR=2.96, 99%CI: 2.31–3.86; asexual: OR=1.30, 99%CI: 1.01–1.69).

Increased help-seeking willingness was also associated with increased age (OR=1.36, 99%CI: 1.26–1.48) and gender identities of transgender (OR=1.81, 99%CI: 1.11–3.14), genderqueer (OR=1.83, 99%CI: 1.13–3.18), nonbinary (OR=1.47, 99%CI: 1.18–1.85) relative to cisgender woman. Among campus characteristics, attending a private college (OR=1.21, 99%CI: 1.13–1.29) and having a positive campus culture (OR=1.51, 99%CI: 1.38–1.64) were both associated with greater help-seeking willingness. In terms of mental health characteristics, greater mental health distress, whether moderate (OR=1.18, 99%CI: 1.11–1.26) or severe (OR=1.08, 99%CI: 1.02–1.14) and suicide risk (OR=1.18, 99%CI: 1.11–1.24) were associated with greater help-seeking willingness.

Individual risk factors for lower help-seeking willingness included cisgender man (OR=0.44, 99%CI: 0.42–0.47) or other gender identity (OR=0.54, 99%CI: 0.38–0.79) relative to cisgender woman; Asian (OR=0.69, 99%CI: 0.65–0.74), Black (OR=0.81, 99%CI: 0.71–0.93), Hispanic (OR=0.80, 99%CI: 0.74–0.86), NAPI (OR=0.76, 99%CI: 0.65–0.89), or other (OR=0.70, 99%CI: 0.57–0.85), relative to White; and having other/unknown (OR=0.59, 99%CI: 0.51–0.70) or no insurance (OR=0.68, 99%CI: 0.71–0.85) relative to school insurance.

### Help-Seeking Willingness and Differences

Table 3 displayed multilevel logistic regression results, before and after controlling for help-seeking history. Even after controlling for help-seeking history, greater odds of help-seeking willingness persisted for gay (AOR=2.01, 99%CI: 1.63–2.49), bisexual (AOR=1.35, 99%CI: 1.23–1.49), questioning (AOR=1.22, 99%CI: 1.04=1.45), pansexual (AOR=1.31, 99%CI: 1.06=1.63), and queer (AOR=1.78, 99%CI: 1.35=2.38) students relative their heterosexual counterparts.

Meanwhile, relative to heterosexual students, lesbian (OR=1.31, 99%CI: 1.07=1.62) and non-heterosexual other (OR=1.40, 99%CI: 0.96–2.09) students had elevated odds of help-seeking willingness that attenuated after controlling for help-seeking history. The elevated odds of help-seeking willingness detected for Hispanic (AOR=0.81, 99%CI: 0.74–0.87), multiracial (AOR=0.87, 99%CI: 0.78–0.98) and other (AOR=0.79, 99%CI: 0.64–0.97) relative to White students also attenuated. Additionally, adjusting for help-seeking history reversed the associations of mental health characteristics and elevated help-seeking willingness. Severe mental health distress (AOR=0.74, 99%CI: 0.69–0.8) and positive suicide risk (AOR=0.79, 99%CI: 0.73–0.85) became associated with decreased help-seeking willingness in the fully adjusted model.

### Help-Seeking History and Differences

Table 4 examined 12-month and lifetime help-seeking history and their associations with characteristics including sexual orientation. Even after adjusting for mental health needs such as mental health distress level and suicide risk, all sexual minority groups had elevated odds of 12-month and lifetime help-seeking history relative to heterosexual students.

Beyond sexual orientation, moderate (AOR=1.60, 99% CI: 1.51–1.71) and severe (AOR=1.99, 99%CI: 1.86–2.12) levels of mental health distress and positive suicide risk (AOR=2.09, 99%CI: 1.97–2.21) were associated with greater 12-month help-seeking history. Students with moderate (AOR=1.47, 99%CI: 1.40–1.57) and severe (AOR=1.7, 99%CI: 1.60–1.81) distress levels and positive suicide risk (AOR=2.38, 99%CI: 2.25–2.51) also had greater lifetime help-seeking history.

## DISCUSSION

Mental health service studies have largely focused on help-seeking intention and history 10,37. Few college health studies have examined help-seeking willingness, especially among populations with high mental health needs, such as sexual minority students 38. Addressing this literature gap, we assessed college students’ help-seeking willingness by sexual orientation. We detected increased help-seeking willingness for students with a positive help-seeking history and for several sexual minority student groups relative to heterosexual students. After controlling for help-seeking history, associations with increased help-seeking willingness persisted for gay, bisexual, questioning, pansexual, and queer students, but attenuated for lesbian and non-heterosexual other students. All sexual minority groups, including lesbian and non-heterosexual other students, had elevated odds of both 12-month and lifetime help-seeking history relative to heterosexual students, even after controlling for mental health characteristics.

### Mental Health Characteristics, Help-Seeking History, and Help-Seeking Willingness

Help-seeking history was the strongest predictor of help-seeking willingness identified by this study. Students who sought help within the past 12 months had a 7.4 higher odds of help-seeking willingness than students who never sought help. Worse mental health characteristics, including distress level and suicide risk, were associated with greater help-seeking history and willingness. However, when we adjusted for help-seeking history in our model for help-seeking willingness, the association reversed, and worse mental health characteristics became associated with decreased help-seeking willingness. This finding suggests that help-seeking history was an important mediator between mental health needs and help-seeking willingness. Students with greater mental health needs had decreased help-seeking willingness, but they also had elevated help-seeking behavior which strongly predicted help-seeking willingness and reversed the poor help-seeking willingness among this group.

Reassuringly, students with poor mental health were more likely to have a positive help-seeking history and hence be connected with care. However, students with poor mental health who were not been connected with care had decreased help-seeking willingness. Our findings show that even a remote help-seeking history beyond 12 months significantly improved one’s help-seeking willingness. Establishing a help-seeking history for students with poor mental health should be an intervention priority.

### Greater Help-Seeking Willingness Among Most Sexual Minority Students

Help-seeking willingness was a resilience factor uniquely associated with many sexual minority student groups, including gay, bisexual, questioning, pansexual, and queer. This finding was striking as most associations, with protective characteristics identified in bivariate analysis, attenuated after controlling for help-seeking history. One possible explanation is that these sexual minority groups were more likely to have social environments and cultural norms supportive of mental health help-seeking 11. Furthermore, formal campus resources such as LGBQ+-focused community centers and resources help to address the specific mental health needs of sexually diverse individuals, relieve stigma, create an environment of trust, and permit greater sharing of knowledge about mental health 39. Further research should explore the etiology of increased help-seeking willingness among sexual minority students and how this resilience factor could be incorporated into interventions for other groups.

Distinct from other sexual minority groups, after controlling for help-seeking history, the lesbian identity was no longer associated with increased help-seeking willingness. Increased help-seeking willingness among lesbian students was largely driven by their help-seeking history and this rather than the identity-specific characteristics and resources identified for other sexual minority groups. Lesbian students may have social groups or cultural norms on mental health more similar to heterosexual students. Another explanation is that campus health resources provide more limited mental health resources to lesbian students compared to other sexual minority identities. However, as limited studies on help-seeking disaggregated lesbians from the rest of the LGBQ+ group, it remains equivocal why lesbian students have help-seeking willingness comparable to heterosexual students rather than other sexual minority students. Focused qualitative studies can help illuminate the lived experiences of help-seeking for lesbian students and how they differ from other sexual minority groups. Mental health studies need to disaggregate among sexual minority groups to understand variation by diverse sexual orientations.

Importantly, the detected greater help-seeking willingness for many sexual minority groups does not necessarily mean that sexual minority students receive the care that they need. Studies have consistently demonstrated inferior quality of care received by sexual minority college students 40,41. The reassurance of help-seeking willingness among sexual minority students should not dissuade continued investment in sex- and gender-affirming mental health care. Institutions must continue to invest in sex- and gender-informed training for providers and structural competencies that reduce disparities faced by sexual minority students 39,42. Nonetheless, we highlight help-seeking willingness as a mental health resilience factor unique to certain sexual minority groups. We advocate for research on more resilience factors to better understand the strength of minority communities.

### Greater Help-Seeking History among Sexual Minority Students

To further assess help-seeking within sexual minority groups and across sexual orientations, we assessed help-seeking history by sexual orientation. Relative to heterosexual students, all sexual minority groups including lesbian students had increased help-seeking history, even after adjusting for mental health distress level and suicide risk. Previous studies similarly identified greater help-seeking history among sexual minority groups, but most did not control for mental health characteristics 43. As we adjusted for mental health characteristics, we found that the greater help-seeking history among sexual minority students may be driven by identity-related characteristics rather than their disproportionately high mental health burden 2,23,30. However, we understand that our selected mental health characteristics may not fully encapsulate all mental health symptoms and challenges and overlook potential mental health characterstics as the moderator of the association between sexual minority identities and help-seeking history.

### Limitations

While this study makes unique contributions, it has several limitations. First, our survey relies on voluntary self-reporting, which can be prone to response and recall bias. Driven by readiness of disclosure and willingness to seek services, these biases may limit the interpretation of our prevalence rates. Second, the survey design of NCHA may limit the survey’s generalizability. NCHA relies on voluntary response from a select group of participating schools where certain demographics may be over-represented. Nevertheless, the NCHA study has been verified by percentage comparisons, item reliability, and validity analyses with three separate population-level surveys of U.S. college-age students 44. The variety of validation studies increases our confidence that our findings can represent U.S. college students overall. Furthermore, the proportions of sexual minority groups within this dataset are generally consistent with recent polls on sexual orientations among Generation Z Americans 45. As college mental health services may be more identity-affirming than outside service environments, our findings may be specific to sexual minority students on college campuses. Further research is needed to understand help-seeking willingness for students outside of the college environment. Finally, though sexual orientations and other characteristics are self-reported, the categorization of identities can ultimately be broad and does not capture the complex, nuanced experiences that individuals face.

## CONCLUSIONS

Sexual minority students have high rates of mental health problems and this study reports on whether sexual minority students would seek help when needed. Help-seeking history was a strong predictor of help-seeking willingness, and most associations to increased help-seeking willingness attenuated after adjusting for help-seeking history. However, gay, bisexual, questioning, pansexual, and queer students had persistently elevated odds of help-seeking willingness, relative to heterosexual students.

Our study highlights help-seeking willingness as a mental health resilience factor unique to some sexual minority groups. Further research should also seek to elucidate the specific protective factors that yield greater help-seeking willingness for these sexual minority groups, and resultantly develop interventions that promote these factors for other clinically vulnerable populations, such as students with poor mental health but no help-seeking history.
